newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia raises alarm over surge in drug-taking.
newsitem.headline: Russia raises alarm over surge in drug-taking.

text.p: Around two million Russians regularly take illegal drugs and as many as 15 percent of the vast country's 150 million people have had contact with narcotic substances, interior ministry officials said on Tuesday.
They complained that law-enforcement agencies were desperately short of funds to prevent the spread of drugs which leads to growth in crime rate and AIDS infection.

"The number of people consuming drugs in our country has increased more than twofold in the past decade. The rate of increase is especially high among young people," said Alexander Sergeyev of the ministry's anti-drugs department.

"All the figures point to a very negative tendency," he told a news conference. He called for tougher penalties against drug traffickers and more financial resources to help combat the problem and to protect Russia's long international borders.
Sergeyev said that so far attempts to curb the flourishing drug business have foundered on cash shortages and a lack of the needed legislation.
"Due to economic and social reasons not a kopeck of the 85 billion roubles allocated for the (anti-drug) programme in the budget arrived," he said.
"The State Duma (lower house of parliament) has failed to approve laws which could help fight the illegal drugs traffic."
Profits from the production and sale of drugs topped three trillion roubles ($554 million) in 1995. That figure had already been exceeded in the first three months of this year, he said.
"About 80,000 crimes linked to drugs were committed in 1995, up from some 16,000 in 1990," he said, adding that the figures probably represented only the tip of the iceberg.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted a senior health ministry official as saying that the rise in drug consumption had triggered a dramatic growth of AIDS cases among addicts.
The official cited the example of the western enclave of Kaliningrad on the Baltic Sea, between Lithuania and Poland, where the number of AIDS cases rose from 27 in March to 130 now.
He added that in the same period the number of infected drug addicts rose from one to 111.

In Soviet times, drug abuse was officially non-existent but has grown rapidly in recent years, helped by the proliferation of organised criminal networks and the emergence of a wealthy class of Russians able to afford drugs.
More than half of the drugs consumed in the Russian Federation are imported. Rail is the favoured smuggling route.

Sergeyev said Russian drug takers were increasingly switching from traditional drugs like hashish to more costly substances like heroin and cocaine. Synthetic substances like ecstasy were also gaining popularity, he added.

Much of the opium, hashish and marijuana consumed in Russia came from Afghanistan and the former Soviet republics of central Asia. The Golden Triangle of southeast Asia supplies much of the heroin and Latin America the cocaine.
Seizures of opium rose by 70 percent in the first six months of 1996 against the same period last year, exceeding for the first time the amount of marijuana seized, he said.
Sergeyev said Russia's drug squad was cooperating more closely with the authorities in other countries, including the United States and western Europe.

He said the Russian authorities were firmly against the decriminalisation of any drug. The experience of countries like the Netherlands that have taken a more liberal stance showed, he argued, that legalising certain substances did not eliminate the problems of addiction or of drugs-related crime. ($1=5,415 roubles)
